Unit-Wise Weightage & Syllabus Focus

Important change from old papers

Older GTU papers belong mainly to 3110002 - English. The latest material is BE02000021 - English for Technical Communication. Therefore, old papers should be used mainly for grammar, word formation, phonetics and writing practice.

Approx. weightage: 17%

Unit 1: Introduction to Technical Communication

  • Difference between technical and general communication.

  • Synonyms, antonyms, prefixes and suffixes.
  • Parts of speech, tenses, articles, subject-verb agreement and active/passive voice.
Approx. weightage: 20%

  • Writing styles: definition, description, classification and comparison.
  • Paragraph, précis, proofreading, story completion and formal letters.

What the papers are really asking

Paper Pattern and Trend

🧭

GTU exam structure

  • The end-semester paper is of 70 marks.
  • Latest papers commonly have five main questions of 14 marks each.
  • Each question usually contains subparts of 3 marks, 4 marks and 7 marks.
  • OR options are available, but units are mixed, so selective preparation is risky.
🎯

Latest paper priority

  • The latest code is BE02000021 - English for Technical Communication. Latest papers give direct weight to communication cycle, listening, presentation, technical/general communication, reading and literature.
📚

Old paper value

  • Old 3110002 papers still matter because grammar, word formation, phonetics, letters, emails, memos, précis and paragraphs repeat strongly.
⭐

Highest scoring areas

  • Grammar and writing formats can be prepared with fixed rules. They are easier to score than random vocabulary if practiced properly.
✍️

Do not ignore theory

  • The new syllabus asks 7-mark theory answers from communication, listening, reading, presentation and literature. Prepare definitions plus explanation plus examples.
Score-focused plan

Preparation Strategy

30-Day Plan

1
Days 1-5: Communication theory: cycle, types, technical communication and technical vs general communication.
2
Days 6-10: Vocabulary and grammar: word formation, prefixes/suffixes, abbreviations, articles, tenses, SVA, prepositions and active-passive.
3
Days 11-15: Phonetics and speaking: IPA, transcription, diphthongs, organs of speech, presentation and group discussion.
4
Days 16-20: Writing practice: précis, letter, memo, email, paragraph, story, introduction and conclusion.
5
Days 21-24: Listening and reading: types, barriers, effective listener traits, skimming, scanning and comprehension.
6
Days 25-27: Literature: prepare title, theme, character, ending and personal-opinion answers for each story.
7
Days 28-30: Solve latest paper first, revise priority questions, then attempt one old paper for grammar/writing speed.

7-Day Emergency Plan

  • Day 1: Communication cycle, types and technical/general communication.
  • Day 2: Word formation, prefixes/suffixes, abbreviations and common vocabulary.
  • Day 3: Grammar blanks and sentence correction from previous papers.
  • Day 4: Phonetics, transcription and presentation/GD.
  • Day 5: Letter, email, memo, précis and story formats.
  • Day 6: Listening, reading and literature.
  • Day 7: Definitions, priority questions and one timed practice paper.

Full Marks Writing Habits

  • For 7-mark theory answers, write definition, explanation, points, example and conclusion.
  • For grammar, always rewrite the full corrected sentence.
  • For practical writing, correct format is half the battle: subject, salutation, body and closing must be neat.
  • For literature, answer the asked angle: title, sacrifice, ending, character, theme or personal opinion.
  • For phonetics, keep symbols clean and do not overwrite.

Most Important Topics Unit-Wise

Unit 1: Technical Communication

  • Communication cycle with labeled diagram is the most important 7-mark answer.
  • Technical communication vs general communication is repeated in latest papers.
  • Types of communication, especially non-verbal communication, must be prepared with examples.
  • Professional situations: choosing correct communication type, interpersonal and intercultural communication.
  • Noise/barriers, feedback and clarity can be used as supporting points in many answers.

  • Word formation is the strongest repeated area: blending, clipping, compounding, derivation, coining, borrowing and creative respelling.
  • Grammar blanks appear repeatedly: articles, prepositions, tenses, verb forms, modals and subject-verb agreement.
  • Prepare active-passive voice, phrase-clause, parts of speech and sentence structures.

  • Formal letter formats repeat: acknowledgement, apology, complaint, order, adjustment and due-payment letters.
  • Memo and email writing appear repeatedly in old and latest paper patterns.
  • Paragraph, introduction, conclusion, abstract and story completion should be practiced with time limits.

  • IPA transcription is a high-frequency paper area. Practice common paper words first.

Answer Writing Frames

Communication Cycle Flow

Use this sequence when you draw the diagram and explain it:

Sender→Encoding→Message→Channel→Receiver→Decoding→Feedback

Communication Cycle

  • Definition of communication.
  • Neat diagram: sender → encoding → message → channel → receiver → decoding → feedback.
  • Explain each element in one or two lines.
  • Mention noise/context.
  • Add example and conclusion.

Technical vs General Communication

  • Define both terms.
  • Compare purpose, audience, language, tone, format, accuracy and examples.
  • Use a clean two-side comparison in the answer sheet.
  • End with importance of technical communication in engineering.

Word Formation

  • Define the process.
  • Explain how the word is formed.
  • Give at least two examples.
  • If comparison is asked, mention difference clearly.
  • Conclude with vocabulary development.

Précis

  • Read passage and identify main idea.
  • Remove examples, repetition and extra details.
  • Write one-third length in your own words.
  • Keep original meaning unchanged.
  • Give a clear title.

Letter / Memo / Email

  • Use proper format.
  • State purpose in first line.
  • Give details in short paragraphs.
  • Use polite professional tone.
  • End with expected action or thanks.

Literature

  • Name story and author.
  • State theme.
  • Explain relevant event/character.
  • Connect to title, irony, sacrifice, suspense or message.
  • End with personal/critical view if asked.

Important definitions and terms

Exam-Ready Glossary

How to Use This Glossary

For 3 marks: write the definition plus one example. For 4 marks: add two features or exam keywords. For 7 marks: add explanation, types/steps, example and conclusion.

Communication

DefinitionCommunication is the process by which information, ideas, feelings or instructions are exchanged between two or more people through a common system of signs, words, symbols, gestures or behavior.

Exam expansionIn exam answers, mention sender, receiver, message, channel and feedback. A good answer should also say that communication becomes effective only when the receiver understands the message in the intended sense.

ExampleA project manager explaining safety rules to a trainee engineer and receiving confirmation from the trainee.

Technical Communication

DefinitionTechnical communication is the planned and precise communication of technical, scientific or professional information to a specific audience for a specific purpose.

Exam expansionIt is objective, clear, concise, accurate, audience-oriented and often supported by diagrams, reports, manuals, emails, presentations or instructions.

ExampleA user manual, project report, laboratory instruction, product specification or maintenance guide.

Communication Cycle

DefinitionThe communication cycle is the complete path through which a message travels from sender to receiver and returns through feedback.

Exam expansionWrite the sequence: sender, encoding, message, channel, receiver, decoding, feedback and noise/context. This is a compulsory diagram-based answer, so draw it neatly.

ExampleTeacher explains an assignment, students understand it, ask questions and submit the work.

Encoding

DefinitionEncoding is the process of converting an idea or thought into words, symbols, gestures, images or signs before sending it to the receiver.

Exam expansionA sender must encode the message according to audience level. Poor encoding creates confusion even when the idea is correct.

ExampleExplaining Ohm's law using simple words and a circuit diagram for first-year students.

Decoding

DefinitionDecoding is the process by which the receiver interprets the symbols, words or signals received from the sender and understands their meaning.

Exam expansionEffective decoding depends on language knowledge, attention, context and background understanding.

ExampleA student interpreting a teacher's diagram and understanding the concept.

Feedback

DefinitionFeedback is the response given by the receiver to the sender after understanding or reacting to the message.

Exam expansionFeedback completes the communication cycle and helps the sender know whether the message was understood correctly.

ExampleNodding, asking a doubt, sending a reply email or submitting confirmation.

Noise

DefinitionNoise is any disturbance that interferes with the transmission, reception or understanding of a message.

Exam expansionNoise may be physical, psychological, semantic, cultural or technical. Mention remedies such as clarity, proper channel, active listening and feedback.

ExampleLoud classroom noise, poor internet connection, unfamiliar technical terms or mental stress.

Verbal Communication

DefinitionVerbal communication is communication through words, either spoken or written.

Exam expansionIt includes speeches, conversations, meetings, reports, letters, emails and notices. It is useful when exact information must be conveyed.

ExampleA formal email to the Head of Department requesting permission for lab equipment.

Non-verbal Communication

DefinitionNon-verbal communication is the exchange of meaning without words through facial expressions, gestures, posture, eye contact, body language, appearance, tone and silence.

Exam expansionIt supports or contradicts verbal communication. In presentations, non-verbal communication strongly affects confidence and audience interest.

ExampleMaintaining eye contact and open posture during a technical presentation.

Technical vs General Communication

DefinitionGeneral communication is used for everyday social interaction, while technical communication is used to convey specialized information clearly to a defined audience.

Exam expansionCompare purpose, audience, tone, vocabulary, structure, accuracy and examples. Technical communication is formal, objective and task-oriented.

ExampleCasual talk about a mobile phone is general; a mobile repair manual is technical.

Listening

DefinitionListening is an active mental process of receiving, understanding, interpreting, evaluating and responding to spoken messages.

Exam expansionIt is different from hearing because it requires attention and understanding. For 7 marks, add types, traits and barriers.

ExampleListening to faculty instructions and noting important exam guidelines.

Hearing

DefinitionHearing is the physical ability to receive sound through ears. It is automatic and does not always involve understanding.

Exam expansionIn comparison answers, write that hearing is passive and biological, whereas listening is active and intellectual.

ExampleHearing noise in the corridor without paying attention to it.

Active Listening

DefinitionActive listening is listening with full concentration, interest and response so that the speaker feels understood and the message is correctly received.

Exam expansionMention eye contact, nodding, questioning, avoiding interruption, summarizing and removing distractions.

ExampleA team leader listening carefully to a trainee's technical issue before suggesting a solution.

Barriers to Listening

DefinitionBarriers to listening are factors that prevent a listener from receiving or understanding a message effectively.

Exam expansionInclude physical noise, lack of interest, prejudice, language difficulty, information overload, poor speaker delivery and emotional disturbance.

ExampleA student missing important instructions because of mobile distraction.

Skimming

DefinitionSkimming is a rapid reading technique used to understand the general idea or overall meaning of a text without reading every word.

Exam expansionIt is useful before detailed reading, while revising, or while identifying the main theme of a passage.

ExampleReading headings and first sentences to understand a passage quickly.

Scanning

DefinitionScanning is a rapid reading technique used to locate specific information such as names, dates, numbers, keywords or facts.

Exam expansionIt is useful in comprehension questions when the answer is directly present in the passage.

ExampleLooking through a notice to find the exam date and time.

Précis

DefinitionA précis is a concise and clear summary of a given passage written in one's own words, usually about one-third of the original length.

Exam expansionA scoring précis includes a suitable title, main idea, logical flow and no unnecessary examples or personal opinion.

ExampleReducing a 300-word passage on technology into about 100 words with the title 'Impact of Technology'.

Coherence

DefinitionCoherence is the logical arrangement and smooth flow of ideas in writing so that the reader can easily follow the meaning.

Exam expansionUse linking words, proper sequence and relevant supporting details to create coherence.

ExampleFirst explaining a problem, then causes, effects and solution.

Proofreading

DefinitionProofreading is the careful checking of written work to remove errors in spelling, grammar, punctuation, capitalization, word choice and format.

Exam expansionIt is important in professional communication because small errors can reduce credibility.

ExampleCorrecting 'their is many peoples' to 'There are many people'.

Compounding

DefinitionCompounding is a word formation process in which two or more independent words are joined to form a new word.

Exam expansionGive examples and explain meaning change. It is a frequent short-answer topic.

Examplenotebook, book fair, switchboard, keyboard.

Clipping

DefinitionClipping is a word formation process in which a longer word is shortened without changing its basic meaning.

Exam expansionMention common types such as front clipping, back clipping and middle clipping if asked in detail.

Examplelab from laboratory, maths from mathematics, phone from telephone.

Blending

DefinitionBlending is a word formation process in which parts of two words are combined to create a new word.

Exam expansionIt is different from compounding because complete words are not joined; only parts are mixed.

Examplebrunch from breakfast and lunch, motel from motor and hotel.

Borrowing

DefinitionBorrowing is the process of taking a word from another language and using it in English.

Exam expansionBorrowed words show cultural contact and vocabulary expansion.

Examplekhaki, restaurant, bungalow, guru.

Coining

DefinitionCoining is the creation of a new word, often through brand names, inventions, technology or popular usage.

Exam expansionSome coined words become common nouns after frequent public use.

ExampleXerox, Google, selfie.

Creative Respelling

DefinitionCreative respelling is intentionally changing the normal spelling of a word for style, branding or attention.

Exam expansionIt is common in advertisements and brand names.

ExampleKoffee instead of coffee, FeviKwik.

Abbreviation

DefinitionAn abbreviation is a shortened form of a word or phrase.

Exam expansionIt saves time and space in technical and formal writing. It may use initial letters or shortened spelling.

ExampleDr. for Doctor, Eng. for Engineer.

Acronym

DefinitionAn acronym is a word formed from the initial letters of a phrase and pronounced as a word.

Exam expansionDo not confuse acronyms with simple abbreviations. In exams, full forms are often asked.

ExampleNASA, AIDS, WiFi.

Phonetics

DefinitionPhonetics is the scientific study of speech sounds, including how they are produced, transmitted and heard.

Exam expansionIn GTU papers it is linked with IPA, transcription, vowels, consonants and organs of speech.

ExampleStudying the difference between /i:/ in seat and /ɪ/ in sit.

IPA

DefinitionIPA stands for International Phonetic Alphabet, a standard system of symbols used to represent the pronunciation of words accurately.

Exam expansionIt helps learners pronounce words correctly even when spelling is confusing.

Examplebook /bʊk/, water /ˈwɔːtər/.

Diphthong

DefinitionA diphthong is a vowel sound in which the tongue glides from one vowel position to another within the same syllable.

Exam expansionGive at least four examples if asked: /eɪ/, /aɪ/, /ɔɪ/, /əʊ/, /aʊ/.

Exampleday /deɪ/, boy /bɔɪ/, now /naʊ/.

Articulation

DefinitionArticulation is the process of producing speech sounds by using speech organs such as lips, tongue, teeth, palate and vocal cords.

Exam expansionFor detailed answers, explain place and manner of articulation.

Example/p/ is produced by closing both lips and releasing air.

Presentation

DefinitionA presentation is a planned oral communication delivered before an audience to inform, explain, demonstrate or persuade.

Exam expansionA good presentation has audience analysis, clear opening, organized body, conclusion, visual aids, confident delivery and body language.

ExamplePresenting an engineering project model in class.

Group Discussion

DefinitionA group discussion is a structured conversation in which participants exchange views on a given topic to test knowledge, communication, leadership and teamwork.

Exam expansionFor tips, mention listening, relevant points, respectful disagreement, examples, time awareness and conclusion.

ExampleDiscussing 'Artificial Intelligence in Engineering Education'.

Memo

DefinitionA memo is a short internal official message used within an organization to inform, remind, warn or instruct employees.

Exam expansionA memo should have To, From, Date, Subject and a clear message body.

ExampleWarning memo about frequent breaks during working hours.

Email

DefinitionAn email is an electronic message used for fast written communication in academic and professional contexts.

Exam expansionA good email has clear subject, salutation, concise body, polite tone, closing and sender details.

ExampleEmail to project manager requesting one week leave.

Compiled from the supplied GTU syllabus and supplied books.

Matrices

Formula/TheoremProper Mathematical Form
Rank\(\operatorname{Rank}(A)=\) number of non-zero rows in REF/RREF \(=\) order of largest non-zero minor.
Gauss-Jordan Inverse\([A\mid I] ightarrow[I\mid A^{-1}]\), if \(A\) is non-singular.
Eigenvalue\(\det(A-\lambda I)=0\). Non-zero vector \(X\) satisfying \(AX=\lambda X\) is an eigenvector.
DiagonalizationIf \(A\) has \(n\) linearly independent eigenvectors, then \(P^{-1}AP=D\), where \(P\) has eigenvectors as columns.
Cayley-Hamilton TheoremEvery square matrix satisfies its characteristic equation: \(p(A)=0\).
Orthogonal Matrix\(A^TA=I\), therefore \(A^{-1}=A^T\).

First-Order ODE

Formula/TheoremProper Mathematical Form
Exact Equation\(M\,dx+N\,dy=0\) is exact if \( rac{\partial M}{\partial y}= rac{\partial N}{\partial x}\).
Integrating Factor in \(x\)If \( rac{M_y-N_x}{N}=f(x)\), then \(IF=e^{\int f(x)\,dx}\).
Integrating Factor in \(y\)If \( rac{N_x-M_y}{M}=g(y)\), then \(IF=e^{\int g(y)\,dy}\).
Linear Differential Equation\( rac{dy}{dx}+P(x)y=Q(x)\), where \(IF=e^{\int P(x)\,dx}\). Solution: \(y\cdot IF=\int Q(x)\cdot IF\,dx+C\).
Bernoulli Equation\( rac{dy}{dx}+Py=Qy^n\). Put \(v=y^{1-n}\).
Clairaut Equation\(y=px+f(p)\), where \(p= rac{dy}{dx}\). General solution: \(y=Cx+f(C)\). Singular solution is obtained from envelope.

Higher-Order ODE

Formula/TheoremProper Mathematical Form
Auxiliary EquationFor \(F(D)y=X\), solve \(F(m)=0\) to find the complementary function.
Repeated RootIf root \(m\) is repeated \(r\) times, then CF contains \(e^{mx},xe^{mx},x^2e^{mx},\ldots,x^{r-1}e^{mx}\).
Complex RootsIf roots are \(\alpha\pm i eta\), then \(CF=e^{\alpha x}(C_1\cos eta x+C_2\sin eta x)\).
Variation of ParametersFor \(y''''+Py''+Qy=R\), \(y_p=-y_1\int rac{y_2R}{W}\,dx+y_2\int rac{y_1R}{W}\,dx\).
Euler-Cauchy EquationTry \(y=x^m\). Example: \(x^2y''''+axy''+by=0\) gives \(m(m-1)+am+b=0\).
Power Series MethodAssume \(y=\sum a_nx^n\), substitute, compare powers, and find recurrence relation.

Complex Differentiation

Formula/TheoremProper Mathematical Form
Cauchy-Riemann EquationsFor \(f(z)=u(x,y)+iv(x,y)\), \( rac{\partial u}{\partial x}= rac{\partial v}{\partial y}\) and \( rac{\partial u}{\partial y}=- rac{\partial v}{\partial x}\).
Derivative\(f''(z)=u_x+iv_x=v_y-iu_y\), when CR equations hold and partial derivatives are continuous.
Harmonic FunctionA function \(u\) or \(v\) is harmonic if \( rac{\partial^2u}{\partial x^2}+ rac{\partial^2u}{\partial y^2}=0\).
Harmonic ConjugateUse \(v_y=u_x\) and \(v_x=-u_y\), then integrate consistently.
Exponential FunctionIf \(z=x+iy\), then \(e^z=e^{x+iy}=e^x(\cos y+i\sin y)\).
Logarithmic Function\(\log z=\log r+i heta\), where \(r=|z|\) and \( heta=\arg z\).

Complex Integration, Residues and Theorems

Formula/TheoremProper Mathematical Form
Cauchy-Goursat TheoremIf \(f(z)\) is analytic in a simply connected domain, then \(\oint_C f(z)\,dz=0\).
Cauchy Integral Formula\(\oint_C rac{f(z)}{z-a}\,dz=2\pi i\,f(a)\), where \(a\) lies inside \(C\).
Derivative Formula\(\oint_C rac{f(z)}{(z-a)^{n+1}}\,dz= rac{2\pi i}{n!}f^{(n)}(a)\).
ResidueThe coefficient of \((z-a)^{-1}\) in the Laurent series of \(f(z)\) about \(z=a\) is called \(\operatorname{Res}(f,a)\).
Simple PoleIf \(a\) is a simple pole, then \(\operatorname{Res}(f,a)=\lim_{z o a}(z-a)f(z)\).
Residue Theorem\(\oint_C f(z)\,dz=2\pi i\sum \operatorname{Res}(f,a_k)\), where \(a_k\) are poles inside \(C\).
Rouché’s TheoremIf \(|g(z)|<|f(z)|\) on \(C\), then \(f(z)\) and \(f(z)+g(z)\) have the same number of zeros inside \(C\).

Summary & Golden Rules

  1. Latest syllabus beats old paper habit. Prepare BE01R00051 first.
  2. Unit 5 is the biggest scoring zone. Do not treat it as light theory.
  3. Unit 2 numericals are predictable. Practice until formulas come automatically.
  4. Every 7-mark theory answer needs a diagram, labelled points, and applications/conclusion.
  5. Definitions should include symbol, unit, and one-line meaning wherever possible.

  8. For billing problems, show units per day, units per month, and rupee amount.
